patch.objective: Interpret the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve, including its shift to the right as temperature, carbon dioxide and acidity rise in working muscle
secondaryObjectives: Explain how ventilation rises with exercise and how chemoreceptors respond to carbon dioxide and pH

sources.cite: OpenStax, Biology 2e, 39.4 Transport of Gases in Human Bodily Fluids
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch: the curve is 'sigmoidal, or S-shaped'; rising CO2 lowers pH, which reduces hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, 'shifting the oxygen dissociation curve to the right'; higher temperature from skeletal muscle activity also reduces affinity. The page did not describe the steep part of the curve; that a small fall in partial pressure there gives a large fall in saturation is the standard reading of an S-shaped curve, marked as the author's. The PTPREREQ course's unit cites OpenStax for this objective.

sources.cite: APTA Acute Care and APTA Cardiovascular and Pulmonary, Adult Vital Sign Interpretation in Acute Care Guide 2021 (boards approved March and April 2021)
sources.note: Relayed from the DPT case icu-early-mobility, which read it 2026-11-11 through a text extraction of the PDF, not re-read: normal exercise response, HR up about 10 beats/min and SBP up about 10 mmHg per MET; stop criteria include an SBP drop over 10 mmHg with increasing workload, new or worsening dysrhythmia, RR over 40, unable to speak comfortably, SpO2 under 90% or a drop of 4% or more.
Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model. Disease courses, effect sizes and local waits are authored and carry FLAG.
